{"rule": "Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and a new passage of about 250 words in the text field.", "text": "Teodor kept the lighthouse the way his mother had kept it, which is to say he lit it at dusk and did not discuss what it was for. The lamp turned once every eleven seconds. He had watched it, by his own loose reckoning, through some nine thousand nights, and he had stopped reckoning because the number had started to sound like a sentence being served.

A woman climbed the path at the last of the light with no bag and shoes wrong for the rocks. She stood at the base of the tower instead of knocking, which told him most of what he needed to know.

"Is this the light for the strait?"

"It's the only light."

"I meant—do the boats see it?"

Teodor struck the match and let the wick take. He had learned that people asked whether the boats saw it when they were waiting for one, and asked whether it was the only light when they had already given up on being found.

"Same light," he said. "Different boats."

She laughed, thin, and folded her arms. Near full dark, the fog came in through the gap in the cliffs and the beam went soft, the way it always did. She stepped closer to the wall.

"Does it always do that?"

"Every night. Same hour."

"Then you'd think it wouldn't bother you."

"You'd think." He trimmed the flame a hair. "But I want it to. The night the fog looks ordinary is the night I stop looking."

A horn sounded, far and low. She didn't move toward the path.

"Tide turns at four," he said. "You don't have to go down yet."

"When do I have to?"

"At four," said Teodor. "That's what the tide is for.""}
